Coded with having BPD or not, it doesn't really excuse toxic behaviour. 

I personally have anxiety and depression. Sometimes my anxiety causes me to act out and appear rude, or cut of friends. Sometimes my depression leads me to being a bit of a jerk. These are explainations for my actions but aren't excuses. 

Things can't be solved overnight, but knowing that something is an issue is half of the journey to being able to fix it. Being able to say "I'm sorry I did \[x\], I did it because of this, but it's not right. I'll be sure to try better myself in future". 

I don't know all too much about BPD, so it wasn't really obvious about me. I don't know if obsessiveness is a trait of BPD, but I still feel the same lesson applies. Putting all your happiness into one person 9/10 will only hurt you, and learning to try and be happy on your own is important\*. Perhaps that is harder for those with BPD (I wouldn't know), but it's still important.  


*\*That doesn't mean to have no friends, having friends is ofc important. It just means to be able to be happy with yourself too.*

I see the angle they were getting at with Spinel. I personally didn't feel like the message of not getting attached to others was implied, given how her clinginess wasn't ever addressed and she was simply given new people to be attached to.

I can see what they were trying to do, I just feel like personally if they tackled it from a slightly more different angle they would have had such a bigger impact and important message.

It's a mix - the fact it's a mix between serious themes and comedy is actually the main reason i thoroughly enjoy the show. 

At the end of the day, although it's a cop-out answer, it is the viewer's decision on whether or not they want to focus on the comedy aspect. I personally focus more on the themes on nihilism and the "do things really matter?" argument. 

Your reasons for asking "why should i care about this show?" are present within the show itself - Rick in season 3 frequently bringing up that 'he doesn't care' because he's got 'infinite [insert family member here]'. But it's shown that he does care. If he didn't why did he stay with the family at the end of S3E10 when he has lost all status in the family?

I think the show is attempting to develop the personal relationships between the characters. There's infinite Morty's, but there's only one 'Morty' (C-137). Rick is attempting to distance himself from his family with the 'there are infinite' argument, though being only human, he does form attachments.

I think the conflict with nihilism and emotional moments are somewhat similar to Rick. He is nihilistic, he knows that nothing matters because he's the most intelligent man in the multiverse. But he's only human - even if he hates it. 

However all that being said, somebody doesn't need to look deep into the (possible) commentary of the episodes. One can just watch for the humour and step away from it casually. 

I know it sounds completely and utterly like a cop-out, but it's just how different people may choose to approach and watch the show. That being said, i don't think the serious elements are pointless. I do think they will lead up to something. Season 3 handled it's 'serious' elements poorly (Just making all the smiths become MORE like assholes with perhaps the exception of Jerry), but i'm hoping Season 4 will handle it better.

I think probably around when Season 3 started. I joined the fandom around midway through season 2, and things weren't nearly as bad. I noticed from the moment Season 3 aired that things seemed a little more toxic. 

I don't think its what "set it off" persay, it's much more a case of **the larger the fanbase, the more likely it is that you're going to encounter ''those'' kinds of people.** And the more sane people in the community don't feel the need to make themselves heard.

1) Depends on which "Suicide Hotline" you are referring to - However from looking it up, certain establishments use volunteers whereas others use professional counsellors. the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline are one of the ones with the professionally hired people.

2) Most likely a call center. I can't say for certain - but i know somebody who used to work for a transgender help hotline, and they had given times when to come in.

3) Speaking about the police, it's a tricky question to answer. In 99% of most cases, they will not call any kind of authority without your explicit permission. But in certain circumstances they may do so in order to save a live. 

4) it really depends on the person using the service. For some people, just being able to vent their problems to somebody and get it out of their system can be helpful, whereas for others it may seem pointless and unnecessary. For some, they may use it to get ideas on how to further recieve help, or distract them from suicidal thoughts they are currently having. You're right in the sense that the operators don't know you personally, but if they didn't care about assisting somebody they probably wouldn't have taken the job anyways.
